inheritance-for-shared-behavior.label: Inheritance for Shared Behavior
inheritance-for-shared-behavior.summary: Use a parent class for genuinely shared state and behavior, then call `super().__init__` when a child constructor adds specialized state.

try_inheritance_for_shared_behavior_sket.title: Make Book inherit shared behavior
try_inheritance_for_shared_behavior_sket.prompt: `CatalogItem` already owns the shared `title` constructor and `label()` method. In `models/book.py`, make `Book` inherit from `CatalogItem`. Do not add a `Book.__init__` or `Book.label()` yet; this exercise is about reusing the parent's existing setup and behavior. Leave `main.py` and `models/catalog_item.py` unchanged.
try_inheritance_for_shared_behavior_sket.hint: Put the parent class in parentheses in the `Book` class header.

help.concept: A child class inherits available parent behavior. With no child constructor or label method, `Book` can use the parent's versions.
help.hint_2: Change only the `Book` class header; keep the body as `pass`.

try_inheritance_for_shared_behavior_sket.title: Add Book-specific state with super()
try_inheritance_for_shared_behavior_sket.prompt: `Book` already inherits from `CatalogItem`. In `models/book.py`, define `__init__(self, title, author)`. Call `super().__init__(title)` so the parent owns the shared title setup, then store the Book-specific author on `self.author`. Do not duplicate `self.title = title` inside `Book`. Leave `main.py` and `models/catalog_item.py` unchanged.
try_inheritance_for_shared_behavior_sket.hint: Let the parent initialize the shared title first, then store only the child-specific author.

help.concept: `super().__init__` lets a child constructor reuse parent setup instead of copying the parent's initialization logic.
help.hint_1: Call the parent constructor with the shared `title` value.
help.hint_2: After the super call, assign `author` to `self.author`.

sc-inheritance-shared-work.title: When does a parent class help?
sc-inheritance-shared-work.prompt: When is inheritance a good fit for shared setup?
sc-inheritance-shared-work.hint: Use a parent for behavior or state that is genuinely common to related child classes.

help.concept: Inheritance is useful when related classes can reuse meaningful shared state or behavior.
help.hint_1: The shared code should belong naturally to the parent concept.
help.hint_2: Do not introduce inheritance just to avoid a few unrelated lines.

options.a: Whenever two unrelated classes happen to contain the same number of lines.
options.b: When related classes genuinely share state or behavior that belongs in one parent.
options.c: Whenever every child must eventually produce identical output.
options.d: Only when no objects will ever be created.

help.concept: `super()` lets the child reuse parent initialization without naming or copying the parent implementation.

sc-inheritance-method-reuse.title: Place shared and specialized state
sc-inheritance-method-reuse.prompt: `CatalogItem` stores `title`, while only `Book` has an `author`. Which design best matches those responsibilities?
sc-inheritance-method-reuse.hint: Put genuinely shared state on the parent and child-only state on the child.

help.concept: A parent owns shared state; a child adds only the state or behavior that makes it more specific.
help.hint_1: Every catalog item needs a title.
help.hint_2: Only books need the author field in this example.

options.a: Store both title and author only on `CatalogItem`, even for non-books.
options.b: Store title independently in every child and leave the parent empty.
options.c: Let `CatalogItem` initialize title, then let `Book` add author after calling `super().__init__(title)`.
options.d: Put both values in `main.py` and keep them off the objects.
